title: Flooding without extra rain: Rubkona and Fangak, 2018-2025
intro: Rainfall over South Sudan has not increased since 2018, but the land has filled with water. Around Bentiu (Rubkona County) and in Fangak, on the western and northern edges of the Sudd wetland, ground that dried out every year until 2020 has stayed flooded since 2021. The steps below show that change in the satellite record and what followed on the ground.

steps.heading: Start with the groundwater trend
steps.text: Choose 'Groundwater' and set 'Show' to the trend view. NASA's groundwater indicator, which feeds GRACE satellite gravity data into a land model, rose in all 79 counties. The national average went from the 4th percentile in 2018, far below the long-term normal, to the 36th percentile in 2025. The 45 counties with a thick dark outline have a statistically significant rise. The Sudd counties are hatched because surface flood water there can be mistaken for groundwater.

steps.heading: Check the rainfall
steps.text: Switch to rainfall, still in the trend view. No county has a significant rainfall trend, and the gauge-blended CHIRPS record agrees. The water came from upstream. Lake Victoria, which feeds the White Nile, rose above its 1964 record level in 2020, 2021 and 2024, and a 2026 study finds that the Sudd's flooded extent follows those lake peaks 9 to 13 months later.

steps.heading: Use the time slider to look at the dry season
steps.text: Choose 'Sudd wetland flooded area', set 'Show' to values in original units, and drag the slider to March, the height of the dry season. In March 2018, 2019 and 2020, less than 0.1% of Rubkona was under water. In March 2022 the figure was 48.5%, and in March 2023 it was 57.4%. Step through the years to see the water arrive in 2021 and stay.

steps.heading: Click Rubkona to see how the ground cooled
steps.text: Switch to 'Daytime ground surface temperature', then hover over Rubkona and click it to open its charts. In March 2018 the ground there reached 42.9 °C by day. In March 2022, with half the county under water, it reached 30.2 °C, and the county's cooling trend (−0.74 °C a year) is significant. The grassland that used to burn every dry season was under water too. Satellites counted 4,105 fires in Rubkona in 2018 and 387 in 2022, and in Fangak 11,197 in 2018 and 94 in 2021.

steps.heading: Turn on the migration arrows
steps.text: Choose the radar flooded-area map, set the slider to August 2022 and turn on the migration arrows for 'Climate: floods and other disasters'. The thickest arrow runs from Fangak to Ayod and stands for 14,000 people displaced by floods that month. IOM recorded more flood displacements in Fangak in 2020-2025 than in any other county, about 174,000. The arrows only show moves between counties. Of Rubkona's roughly 47,500 flood displacements in 2021-2022, just 330 appear as moves to another county, while Rubkona itself took in about 4,300 people fleeing floods elsewhere in 2022.

steps.heading: Compare with hunger
steps.text: Choose 'Share of people facing hunger (IPC 3+)'. In October 2022, 80% of people in both Rubkona and Fangak were in crisis-level hunger or worse. In Fangak that was up from 60-70% in every analysis from 2018 to 2020. In each of the 10 IPC analyses since 2018, the 16 Sudd counties averaged 12 to 21 percentage points more people in crisis than the rest of the country.

steps.heading: Open the national trends
steps.text: Click 'See national trends in aid and socioeconomic outcomes' at the top of the left panel. In 2025, GRACE satellites measured more total water stored in the land than in any year since 2018 (+16.2 cm above normal), and IOM recorded about 242,000 flood displacements. That same year the UN appeal received 46% of what it asked for (US$787 million of US$1.70 billion), and US humanitarian funding fell from US$708 million in 2024 to US$282 million. By September 2025, 80% of people in Fangak were again in crisis-level hunger.

caveat: The data show patterns and cannot prove cause. Hunger, displacement and violence in the Sudd also have political and economic causes. GRACE sees about 300 km at a time, so read it regionally. The radar flood map counts only water beyond each place's normal dry-season state, so ground that stays flooded all year (much of Rubkona since 2021) looks nearly dry on it; the Sudd wetland map shows those areas. NASA IMERG rainfall over Rubkona rises sharply after 2021 (873 mm in 2018, 2,629 mm in 2023) while CHIRPS shows no rise (900 mm and 809 mm), which suggests the satellite is reading standing water as rain. IOM counts displacement movements, so one person can be counted more than once. The Sudd map has no data for July-November 2025.
